candidates.label: Emmaus Nicopolis (Imwas)
candidates.support: About 160 stadia (roughly 30 km) from Jerusalem, matching the reading in the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus; has significant Christian veneration and Byzantine-period archaeological remains, but the distance is difficult to reconcile with a same-day round trip on foot as narrated in Luke 24.

candidates.label: Qaloniya / Motza
candidates.support: About 60 stadia (roughly 11 km) from Jerusalem, matching the distance given in most Greek manuscripts of Luke 24:13; salvage excavations at the site have uncovered a first-century Jewish village, which has led some modern scholars to favor this candidate, though it lacks the long history of Christian commemoration of Emmaus Nicopolis.

candidates.label: El-Qubeibeh
candidates.support: About 60 stadia from Jerusalem; identified with Emmaus mainly from the Crusader period onward and recognized by the Franciscans, but no ancient source calls the site Emmaus.

candidates.label: Abu Ghosh
candidates.support: Identified with Emmaus in the Middle Ages partly on the strength of a large church at the site, though the village is more commonly identified by scholars with the biblical Kiriath-Jearim than with Emmaus.

summary.text: Emmaus is the village to which two disciples were walking on the day of the resurrection, according to Luke 24, when the risen Jesus joined them without being recognized; its identification is disputed, with candidate sites proposed at very different distances from Jerusalem.

history.text: Luke's Gospel states the distance from Jerusalem to Emmaus as 'sixty stadia' in the majority of surviving Greek manuscripts, about 11 kilometers, while the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus reads 'one hundred and sixty stadia,' about 30 kilometers; the two readings underlie much of the modern disagreement over which site is meant.

scripture.textWEB: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.
